transitions.priorTeaching: 421 explicitly separates private profit selection, efficient quantity, CS/PS, transfers and surplus losses. 413/414 teach uniform-price MO and feasible profit maximization.
transitions.newTeaching: 422 teaches separated groups, prevention of resale, common constant MK and sufficient capacity before solving each group's MO=MK. The common-price comparison is given, not falsely claimed to be the global optimal common price.
transitions.boundary: Fixed costs deducted once. Different group prices do not alone establish different elasticities; names or line slope alone do not prove responsiveness. More producer profit need not mean more total surplus. Actual target total quantity stays24 while allocation changes; welfare falls496→480.

transitions.priorTeaching: 412 establishes market boundary and monopoly;413/414 establish falling demand, uniform prices and private optimization;422 explicitly changes to separate group prices.

transitions.priorTeaching: 421 welfare accounting assumed no external effects; Book3 tax lessons supply the price wedge and receipts on actual taxed sales. 423 makes competition/market-power assumptions explicit.
transitions.newTeaching: 424 defines an unpaid third-party cost before constructing social MK above private MK. It evaluates an additional transaction, finds efficient quantity, then applies the familiar tax method to a different welfare ledger.
transitions.boundary: Tax receipts are a transfer, not compensation automatically paid to victims. Remaining damage is still real and must be subtracted. A tax can now raise social surplus because the original market omitted damage; this does not contradict Book3's no-external-effects model.

transitions.priorTeaching: 424 establishes private/social distinction, marginal social comparison, external cost totals and a complete public/third-party ledger. Book3§313 teaches subsidy wedge, all-sale spending and CS/PS using their respective prices.
transitions.newTeaching: 425 defines unpaid benefits to third parties, adds them to private willingness to pay and locates the efficient quantity. It explicitly contrasts the same subsidy with and without those external benefits.
transitions.boundary: Spending and external benefits are distinct even when numerically equal. A lower-subsidy variant breaks that numerical equality. Private benefit+3 and external benefit−7 is a separate fixed-quantity comparison, not a new equilibrium. More production is not always better beyond the efficient quantity.
